# When ggplot and plotly aren't enough

<!-- Show 2-3 D3 charts they couldn't make with ggplotly (d3-graph-gallery.com,
     a Pudding piece, a NYT graphic). Point: full control of every mark and
     every interaction. -->

---

# What is D3?

<!-- A JavaScript library that binds data to elements on the page (SVG) in the
     browser. Not a chart function: you build the chart from parts.
     Contrast: ggplot = grammar + defaults; D3 = parts + total control. -->

---

# Reading a D3 file: four parts

<!-- The mini-lecture's core. Annotate one small real D3 chart (a scatterplot):
       1. the data (where it lives in the file)
       2. the scales (same idea as ggplot scales: data -> pixels)
       3. the axes
       4. the marks (circles/rects/lines) + the event handlers (hover)
     Use code-line-numbers to step through. Goal: they can SUPERVISE Claude,
     not write D3. -->

---

# Directing Claude to build one

<!-- Prompt pattern, shown as a quoted prompt on the slide:
       data + chart type + the takeaway title + constraints
       ("single self-contained d3-chart.html, load D3 from a CDN, embed the
        data in the file") + one interaction beyond hover.
     Same prompt scaffold as hw 11 section 5, now aimed at something custom. -->

---

# Sketch first, then direct

<!-- The human-judgment step: before prompting, sketch on paper what the chart
     should look like and what each interaction does. Claude builds what you
     describe; the design is on you. -->

---

# Gotchas

<!-- Short list:
       - Embed data in the file (opening a local .html can't fetch a local CSV)
       - Load D3 from a CDN, pin the version
       - Open in the browser and check the console for errors
       - It must live next to the .qmd to embed with an iframe -->

---

# How to check a D3 chart

<!-- Same three checks as hw 11: numbers (hover vs. data), axes (units, start
     points, resize the window), claim (does the title say more than the data
     supports?). Add: console errors. -->

# Your work can live on the web

<!-- Why: the final report is a repo that renders on Pages. Today: a tiny demo
     repo, the same steps you'll use for the report.
     Pages serves static files from a repo: our job is to get rendered html
     into the repo. -->

---

# The steps

<!-- Numbered list on one slide:
       1. Create a new PUBLIC repo (GitHub Desktop)
       2. Add index.qmd, _quarto.yml, d3-chart.html
       3. Render the site (quarto render) so docs/ exists
       4. Commit + push
       5. GitHub.com: Settings > Pages > Deploy from a branch > main /docs
       6. Wait 1-2 min, open https://<username>.github.io/<repo>/
     Then the "three things everyone forgets" slide below. -->

---

# Step 1: create the demo repo

<!-- GitHub Desktop: File > New Repository. Publish with "Keep this code
     private" UNCHECKED. (Pages on a free account needs a public repo; this is
     a throwaway demo, not the course repo.) Screenshot. -->

---

# Step 2: tell Quarto to render into `docs/`

<!-- Show _quarto.yml:

       project:
         type: website
         output-dir: docs

     Default is _site/; Pages can only serve from the repo root or /docs, so we
     change it. Also add an empty .nojekyll file in the repo root (Quarto docs
     recommend it for the docs/ approach). TEST ONCE END TO END before class. -->

---

# Step 3: render, then push

<!-- `quarto render` (or Render in Positron) creates docs/. Commit and push
     with GitHub Desktop. Check docs/ is in the diff. -->

---

# Step 4: turn on Pages

<!-- Screenshot of Settings > Pages: Source = Deploy from a branch,
     Branch = main, Folder = /docs. Save. -->

---

# Three things everyone forgets

<!-- 1. Turn Pages on (it's off by default)
     2. Render BEFORE you push (Pages serves what's committed; stale or missing
        docs/ = stale or missing site)
     3. The repo must be public
     + Re-render before every push, or nothing changes on the site. -->

# When a static page isn't enough

<!-- GitHub Pages / D3 = everything runs in the reader's browser; the data is
     fixed at render time. Shiny = a live R session behind the page, so the
     reader can change inputs and R recomputes. Use it when you need real
     compute (models, big data, user-entered input). -->
